questions.stem: Dr. Kaur is a skilled cognitive-behavioral psychologist. At a conference she speaks with a vendor selling biofeedback equipment, who assures her the device is intuitive and that she could begin using it with clients the following week. She buys it and plans to try it with several treatment-resistant clients. Dr. Kaur is:

choices.text: behaving unethically unless she obtains training in biofeedback before using it with clients
behaving ethically, since biofeedback rests on the behavioral principles she already commands
behaving ethically, since psychologists are expected to acquire new skills throughout a career
behaving unethically unless she offers clients a choice between biofeedback and her usual approach

questions.explanation: Standard 2.01 requires psychologists to provide services within their current level of competence, as established by education, training, and experience. Incorporating a new technique is one of the two situations the standard is written for; the training must come first.

whyWrong.b: Biofeedback is related to behavioral technique, but its use requires specific training that adjacent expertise does not supply.
whyWrong.c: Psychologists must indeed acquire new skills under 2.01 and 2.03, but that duty does not license using a technique before the training is obtained.
whyWrong.d: Offering a choice speaks to informed consent and overlooks the prior issue, which is that she is not yet competent to deliver the technique at all.

questions.stem: Under Standards 2.01 and 2.03, a psychologist's acquisition of new knowledge and skills over the course of a career is best described as:

choices.text: permitted at the psychologist's own discretion, provided that existing clients are unaffected
required, though expansion must be undertaken so as to minimize potential harm to clients
discouraged unless the psychologist first completes a formal respecialization programme
required only of psychologists who hold a specialty designation from a certifying board

questions.explanation: The text is explicit that maintaining and expanding competence is not merely permitted — psychologists must do so. The accompanying condition is that expansion minimize potential harm to clients.

whyWrong.a: Framing this as discretionary understates the obligation the two standards impose.
whyWrong.c: Formal respecialization is required for changing specialties, not for ordinary skill acquisition.
whyWrong.d: The obligation is general and does not depend on holding a board specialty designation.

questions.stem: Dr. Oyelaran practices in a remote rural county. A family seeks services for a presentation he has limited experience treating, and no other qualified provider is available within a reasonable distance. Under Standard 2.01(d), he may provide the services if he:

choices.text: obtains written informed consent in which the client acknowledges his limited experience
arranges for a qualified colleague to review each recorded session within seventy-two hours
has closely related training or experience and makes a reasonable effort to obtain the needed competence
limits his work to assessment and refers the family elsewhere for any treatment component

questions.explanation: Standard 2.01(d) covers services that are requested when no one else is available and the psychologist lacks sufficient competence. It permits providing them where the psychologist has closely related training or experience and makes a reasonable effort to obtain the required knowledge and skills.

whyWrong.a: Consent is good practice but is not the condition 2.01(d) attaches to providing the service.
whyWrong.b: Consultation is advisable generally, but this specific supervisory arrangement is not what the provision requires.
whyWrong.d: The provision permits the services rather than requiring that they be split in this way.

questions.stem: Standard 2.01(e) addresses emerging areas in which generally recognized preparatory training standards do not yet exist. It requires psychologists to:

choices.text: refrain from practising in the area until the profession establishes formal training standards
obtain approval from an institutional review board before offering the services to clients
restrict the work to research contexts until the relevant training standards are published
take reasonable steps to protect the welfare of clients, students, and others involved

questions.explanation: Standard 2.01(e) directs psychologists working in emerging areas to take reasonable steps to protect the welfare of clients, students, and others. The implication drawn in the text is that a client must be made aware a technique is new or experimental, with special care taken to protect against harm.

whyWrong.a: The provision contemplates practice in emerging areas rather than prohibiting it.
whyWrong.b: IRB approval governs research, and 2.01(e) is not limited to research settings.
whyWrong.c: Nothing in the provision confines emerging-area work to research contexts.

questions.stem: Dr. Menzies begins using a newly developed treatment protocol for which recognized training standards do not yet exist. Under Standard 2.01(e), the text indicates that she must in particular:

choices.text: make the client aware that the technique is new or experimental
collect systematic outcome data so the protocol can be evaluated
obtain a second opinion confirming that no established treatment would serve
charge a reduced fee reflecting the unproven status of the intervention

questions.explanation: The implication the text draws from 2.01(e) is that when a new or experimental technique is used, the client must be made aware of that fact and special care taken to protect the client from harm.

whyWrong.b: Systematic data collection is good scientific practice but is not what the provision requires of the practitioner.
whyWrong.c: No second-opinion requirement appears in the provision.
whyWrong.d: Fee adjustment is a matter for Standard 6 and is not part of 2.01(e).

questions.stem: Following a factory fire, Dr. Sandoval provides crisis services to survivors despite lacking training in trauma intervention, because no trained provider is available. Under Standard 2.02, she must discontinue the services:

choices.text: as soon as she has completed an introductory continuing-education course in trauma work
as soon as the emergency has ended or appropriate services become available
within thirty days, regardless of whether other providers have become available
once each survivor has been given a written referral to a qualified trauma specialist

questions.explanation: Standard 2.02 permits providing services without the appropriate training in emergencies when alternative providers are unavailable, but requires that they be discontinued as soon as the emergency has ended or appropriate services are available.

whyWrong.a: A brief course does not establish competence and is not the endpoint the standard specifies.
whyWrong.c: The standard sets no fixed period; it ties the endpoint to the emergency and to availability.
whyWrong.d: Issuing referrals does not itself satisfy the condition, which turns on the emergency ending or services becoming available.

questions.stem: A psychologist trained and credentialed in educational psychology wishes to add clinical psychology to her practice. Under Section 1.7 of the General Guidelines for Providers of Psychological Services (APA, 1987), she must:

choices.text: earn a second doctoral degree in the new specialty before offering any of its services
practise only under continuing supervision, since a change of specialty cannot be completed
meet the same subject-matter and professional-skill requirements that apply to doctoral training in the new specialty
obtain a written endorsement from a board diplomate in the specialty she intends to enter

questions.explanation: Psychologists changing or adding a specialty must meet the same subject-matter and professional-skill requirements that apply to doctoral education, training, and experience in the new specialty. Practically, this means completing the relevant coursework and supervised training — not earning a second degree.

whyWrong.a: The text is explicit that a second doctoral degree is not required.
whyWrong.b: A change of specialty is achievable; indefinite supervision is not what the guideline contemplates.
whyWrong.d: No endorsement requirement of this kind appears in the guideline.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the practical reading of the specialty-change requirement described in the text?

choices.text: A second doctoral degree is required, since specialty competence is conferred by the degree itself
Neither a degree nor coursework is required, provided the psychologist is supervised for one year
Only continuing-education credits in the new specialty are required before independent practice
A second doctoral degree is not required, but the coursework and supervised training it would demand are

questions.explanation: The requirement targets substance rather than credential: the psychologist must complete the coursework and supervised training that doctoral preparation in the new specialty would demand, without earning the degree again.

whyWrong.a: The text expressly rejects the need for a second doctoral degree.
whyWrong.b: A fixed period of supervision does not substitute for the subject-matter requirements.
whyWrong.c: Continuing education alone falls well short of doctoral-level subject-matter and skill requirements.

questions.stem: Dr. Achebe is asked to supervise a postdoctoral fellow conducting neuropsychological assessments. Standard 2.05 requires that he:

choices.text: take reasonable steps to ensure the fellow can perform the delegated work competently
apply the criteria the Ethics Code specifies for determining a supervisee's competence
personally countersign every assessment report the fellow produces during the fellowship
verify that the fellow carries independent professional liability insurance

questions.explanation: Standard 2.05 requires psychologists to ensure that those to whom they delegate work can perform it competently. The Code provides no specific criteria; the judgment rests with the psychologist.

whyWrong.b: This is the trap: the Code deliberately supplies no criteria, leaving the judgment to the psychologist.
whyWrong.c: Countersignature may be required by an employer or payer, but 2.05 does not impose it.
whyWrong.d: Insurance is a risk-management matter rather than a requirement of 2.05.

questions.stem: Ladany, Lehrman-Waterman, Molinaro, and Wolgast (1999) asked beginning intern-level supervisees to identify ethical violations by their supervisors. The most frequently cited violation was:

choices.text: supervisors' failure to maintain the confidentiality of the interns' clinical material
inadequate performance evaluation and monitoring of the interns' activities
supervisors requiring interns to perform tasks beyond their level of training
the formation of multiple relationships between supervisors and their supervisees

questions.explanation: Inadequate performance evaluation and monitoring was the most frequently cited violation in that study, which is why the text treats regular performance feedback as a critical element of ensuring supervisee competence.

whyWrong.a: Confidentiality lapses are genuine supervisory violations but were not the most frequently cited in this study.
whyWrong.c: Assigning work beyond a supervisee's training is a real 2.05 concern, but it was not the leading complaint reported.
whyWrong.d: Multiple relationships appear in 2.05, but the study's leading finding concerned evaluation and monitoring.

questions.stem: A psychologist is treating a client whose English is limited. The client's adult daughter offers to serve as interpreter for the sessions. Accepting the offer would be inappropriate primarily because it:

choices.text: delegates clinical work to a person without professional interpreter certification
exceeds the psychologist's own boundaries of competence in cross-cultural practice
creates a multiple relationship likely to limit objectivity or lead to exploitation
requires the client to disclose protected information to an unauthorized third party

questions.explanation: Standard 2.05 prohibits delegating work to a person where doing so creates a multiple relationship with the individual being served that is likely to limit objectivity or lead to exploitation. The daughter's familial role is exactly such a relationship.

whyWrong.a: Lack of certification is a practical concern, but the ethical objection 2.05 raises is the relationship itself.
whyWrong.b: The psychologist's own competence is not what the example turns on.
whyWrong.d: The client could authorize the daughter's involvement; the objection survives that authorization.

questions.stem: The legal doctrine under which supervisors and employers may be held legally responsible for the actions of their supervisees and employees is:

choices.text: contributory negligence, arising from the supervisor's own failure to act
informed consent, extended to cover the supervisory relationship
duty to protect, as articulated in the Tarasoff line of cases
vicarious liability, also known as respondeat superior

questions.explanation: Vicarious liability, or respondeat superior, makes supervisors and employers legally responsible for their supervisees' and employees' actions. It is a legal concept distinct from the ethical requirements of Standard 2.05 itself.

whyWrong.a: Contributory negligence concerns an injured party's own contribution to the harm, not a supervisor's liability for another's acts.
whyWrong.b: Informed consent governs a client's agreement to services and has no bearing on supervisory liability.
whyWrong.c: The duty to protect concerns third parties threatened by a client, a separate doctrine entirely.

questions.stem: According to Simon (1992), the legal determination of vicarious liability ordinarily rests on the disparity in training and experience between the parties and on:

choices.text: the supervisor's right, ability, or responsibility to control the supervisee's actions
whether the supervisor received any direct financial benefit from the supervisee's work
the number of hours of face-to-face supervision that were provided in each working week
whether the supervisee held an independent licence at the time the conduct took place

questions.explanation: Simon identifies two factors: the disparity in training and experience between supervisor and supervisee, and the supervisor's right, ability, or responsibility to control the supervisee's actions.

whyWrong.b: Financial benefit can matter in other liability contexts, but it is not one of the two factors named.
whyWrong.c: The frequency of supervision may bear on the control question but is not itself the stated factor.
whyWrong.d: Licensure status is not among the two determinants Simon identifies.

questions.stem: Dr. Ferreira's employee commits an error while performing delegated clinical work, and the affected client sues both the employee and Dr. Ferreira. Dr. Ferreira's potential exposure in that lawsuit is best understood as:

choices.text: an ethical violation of Standard 2.05, from which legal liability then follows automatically
a legal question of vicarious liability, distinct from her obligations under Standard 2.05
an issue the Ethics Code resolves by allocating the responsibility to the employee alone
a matter outside both ethical and legal frameworks unless she directed the specific act

questions.explanation: The text notes that vicarious liability is a legal liability concept, distinct from the ethical requirements of 2.05. A supervisor may face legal exposure for a supervisee's actions independently of whether the ethical standard was breached.

whyWrong.a: The two frameworks are distinct; an ethical breach does not automatically generate legal liability, nor the reverse.
whyWrong.c: The Ethics Code does not allocate legal responsibility, and 2.05 places duties on the delegating psychologist.
whyWrong.d: Vicarious liability arises without the supervisor having directed the particular act.

questions.stem: Dr. Lindgren is going through a contentious divorce and finds that her concentration during sessions has deteriorated noticeably. Under Standard 2.06, appropriate measures would include all of the following EXCEPT:

choices.text: seeking her own therapy in order to address the personal difficulties she is experiencing
referring the affected clients to other qualified professionals for their continuing care
disclosing the details of the divorce to clients so they can decide whether to continue
consulting a colleague in order to determine the most appropriate course of action to take

questions.explanation: Standard 2.06 lists appropriate measures as seeking therapy, referring clients to other professionals, and consulting another professional to identify the most appropriate action. Disclosing personal details to clients is not among them.

whyWrong.a: Seeking therapy is expressly among the appropriate measures.
whyWrong.b: Referral to other professionals is expressly among the appropriate measures.
whyWrong.d: Consulting another professional to identify the appropriate action is expressly listed.

questions.stem: Standard 2.06 directs psychologists to refrain from initiating a professional activity when:

choices.text: any personal difficulty is present, whatever its likely effect on the professional work
a colleague has formally advised the psychologist that he or she appears to be impaired
the psychologist has begun receiving treatment for a diagnosed psychological condition
there is a significant likelihood that personal problems will interfere with the activity

questions.explanation: The threshold in 2.06 is a significant likelihood that personal problems will prevent the psychologist from performing the activity in a competent manner.

whyWrong.a: The standard is calibrated to likely interference, not to the mere existence of a personal difficulty.
whyWrong.b: No colleague's formal advice is required to trigger the standard.
whyWrong.c: Being in treatment does not itself bar a psychologist from initiating professional activities.

questions.stem: A psychologist who has worked exclusively with adults is asked to begin treating adolescents at his clinic. Standard 2.01 addresses this situation because it covers:

choices.text: serving a population the psychologist has not previously served
the emergency provision of services when alternatives are unavailable
delegating professional work to supervisees and employees
practice in emerging areas without recognized training standards

questions.explanation: Standard 2.01 covers two situations the exam tests directly: incorporating a new technique into practice, and serving a population the psychologist has not previously served. A new age group is the second.

whyWrong.b: The emergency provision is 2.02 and nothing here suggests an emergency.
whyWrong.c: Delegation is governed by 2.05 and is not what this situation involves.
whyWrong.d: Adolescent treatment is well established, so no emerging-area provision applies.

questions.stem: Dr. Bassett wishes to expand her practice into an area adjacent to her training. The text describes which step as advisable in determining what additional preparation she needs and when independent practice becomes appropriate?

choices.text: completing a formal postdoctoral respecialization programme in the adjacent practice area
consulting another professional about the training required and the timing of independent work
notifying her state licensing board of the intended expansion of practice well in advance
restricting the new work to clients who give written experimental-treatment consent first

questions.explanation: The text advises consulting another professional to determine what additional training is needed and when independent practice in the area is appropriate, alongside the requirement that expansion minimize potential harm to clients.

whyWrong.a: Formal respecialization pertains to changing specialties, a heavier requirement than expanding into an adjacent area.
whyWrong.c: No advance notification to the licensing board is described.
whyWrong.d: Experimental-treatment consent belongs to emerging-area practice under 2.01(e).

questions.stem: Two days after a hurricane, Dr. Ramos provides psychological first aid at a shelter despite having no disaster-response training. Three weeks later the shelter closes and a trained disaster-response team is now operating in the area, but several people ask Dr. Ramos to continue seeing them. He should:

choices.text: continue, since a therapeutic relationship has formed and abrupt termination would cause them harm
continue, provided that he simultaneously enrols in disaster-response training coursework
discontinue and assist in transferring their care, since appropriate services are now available
continue with those clients who explicitly consent to being seen by an untrained provider

questions.explanation: Standard 2.02 permits untrained emergency provision only while the emergency persists and alternatives are unavailable. Once the emergency has ended or appropriate services become available, the services must be discontinued.

whyWrong.a: Continuity of care matters, but 2.02 makes the authorization temporary and conditional by design.
whyWrong.b: Enrolling in training does not confer present competence, and the condition permitting the work has lapsed.
whyWrong.d: Client consent does not extend an authorization that 2.02 ties to the emergency and to availability.

questions.stem: A clinic director assigns intake interviews to a psychology technician whose training she has never reviewed, assuming the previous director vetted him. Under Standard 2.05, the director's assumption is problematic because the responsibility for judging the technician's competence:

choices.text: rests with the credentialing body that issued the technician's certificate
is discharged by the clinic's written scope-of-practice policy for technicians
transfers to the previous director, who made the original hiring decision
rests with the psychologist delegating the work, on her own judgment

questions.explanation: Because the Code provides no specific criteria, the judgment of whether a supervisee or employee has the requisite knowledge and skills rests with the psychologist who delegates the work.

whyWrong.a: A credential is evidence a psychologist may weigh, but it does not displace her own judgment.
whyWrong.b: A written policy describes permitted tasks; it does not establish a particular person's competence.
whyWrong.c: The duty attaches to the psychologist delegating the work now, not to a predecessor.

questions.stem: A supervisor meets with her intern weekly but provides no evaluative feedback until the end-of-year written evaluation, which the intern finds highly critical and unexpected. Drawing on the text's discussion of 2.05, this pattern is best characterized as:

choices.text: a known source of ethical complaints, since timely performance feedback is a critical element
acceptable, since a formal written evaluation was in fact completed and delivered as required
a multiple relationship problem arising from the supervisor's dual evaluative and teaching role
a question of vicarious liability rather than an ethical concern about supervisory practice

questions.explanation: The text identifies regular performance feedback as a critical element of ensuring supervisee competence and notes that a lack of timely feedback is a known source of ethical complaints — consistent with the Ladany et al. finding.

whyWrong.b: Completing the annual form does not supply the ongoing feedback the text treats as critical.
whyWrong.c: Evaluation is intrinsic to supervision and does not by itself create a multiple relationship.
whyWrong.d: Vicarious liability concerns legal responsibility for a supervisee's acts, not the adequacy of feedback.

questions.stem: Which provision would a psychologist rely on when asked to provide services she is not fully competent to deliver, where no other provider is available and the situation is not an emergency?

choices.text: Standard 2.02, covering the provision of services in emergencies
Standard 2.01(d), covering services where no one else is available
Standard 2.01(e), covering practice in newly emerging areas
Standard 2.06, covering the effect of personal problems on professional work

questions.explanation: 2.01(d) is the provision for services requested when no one else is available and the psychologist lacks sufficient competence, permitting them where closely related training exists and reasonable effort is made to obtain the needed competence.

whyWrong.a: 2.02 governs emergencies, and the stem specifies the situation is not one.
whyWrong.c: 2.01(e) concerns areas lacking recognized training standards, not unavailability of providers.
whyWrong.d: 2.06 concerns personal problems interfering with professional activity.

questions.stem: Dr. Whitcombe, a school psychologist, is asked by a court to conduct a child custody evaluation, a forensic activity for which he has no training. Several qualified forensic psychologists practise in the region. He should:

choices.text: accept the appointment, since a court request carries an obligation to assist the tribunal
accept it and retain a forensic psychologist to review his report before it is filed
decline and refer the court to a psychologist competent in forensic evaluation
accept it under 2.01(d), since a court appointment establishes that no one else is available

questions.explanation: Standard 2.01 limits practice to services within one's current competence, established by education, training, and experience. Forensic services are named among those the standard covers, and the exceptions do not apply where qualified providers are available.

whyWrong.a: A court request does not confer competence or suspend the boundaries 2.01 imposes.
whyWrong.b: Post hoc review does not make him competent to conduct the evaluation itself.
whyWrong.d: 2.01(d) requires that no one else be available; qualified forensic psychologists practise in the region.

questions.stem: Dr. Yusuf recognizes that a chronic health condition has begun to affect his effectiveness with clients. Standard 2.06 directs him to take "appropriate measures," which the text describes as:

choices.text: suspending his licence voluntarily until the health condition has been medically resolved
notifying his state licensing board of the condition and awaiting its formal determination
reducing his caseload by half and documenting that reduction in each affected client record
seeking therapy, referring clients elsewhere, or consulting another professional about what to do

questions.explanation: Where a physical or psychological problem may adversely affect effectiveness, the appropriate measures the text lists are seeking therapy, referring clients to other professionals, and consulting another professional to identify the most appropriate action.

whyWrong.a: Voluntary licence suspension is not among the measures described and would often be disproportionate.
whyWrong.b: No board-notification requirement is described in this standard.
whyWrong.c: A fixed caseload reduction is not one of the listed measures.

questions.stem: A hospital psychologist delegates psychological testing to a technician she supervises. The technician is competent, but she is also the technician's landlord and holds his lease. Under Standard 2.05, the arrangement is problematic if the relationship:

choices.text: is likely to limit her objectivity or lead to exploitation of the person being served
has not been disclosed in writing to the hospital's compliance department for review
involves any financial dimension whatever between the supervisor and the supervisee
would be prohibited by the licensing statute of the jurisdiction in which she practises

questions.explanation: 2.05 prohibits delegating work to a person where the multiple relationship is likely to limit objectivity or lead to exploitation. The likelihood of that effect, rather than the mere existence of a second relationship, is the test.

whyWrong.b: Disclosure to compliance is institutionally sensible but is not the test 2.05 sets.
whyWrong.c: The standard is not a blanket bar on financial dimensions; it turns on the likely effect.
whyWrong.d: The Ethics Code applies independently of whether a licensing statute reaches the arrangement.

questions.stem: Dr. Petrides, whose training is in health psychology, has agreed to see a client presenting with a condition she has treated only twice. She has related training, no other provider is available locally, and she has arranged weekly consultation with an expert while completing a relevant course. This arrangement is best described as:

choices.text: inconsistent with 2.01, since she may not treat a condition she has encountered only twice
consistent with 2.01(d), given closely related training and reasonable effort to obtain competence
governed by 2.02, which permits services whenever alternative providers are unavailable
permissible only where the client consents in writing to treatment by an inexperienced provider

questions.explanation: 2.01(d) permits the services where the psychologist has closely related training or experience and makes a reasonable effort to obtain the needed knowledge and skills. Consultation plus coursework is the paradigm of that reasonable effort.

whyWrong.a: This reads 2.01 as an absolute bar and ignores the provision written for exactly this situation.
whyWrong.c: 2.02 concerns emergencies; unavailability alone in a non-emergency falls under 2.01(d).
whyWrong.d: The written consent described is not the condition 2.01(d) imposes.

questions.stem: All of the following accurately describe Standard 2.02 EXCEPT:

choices.text: it applies in circumstances where alternative mental health services are not available to the recipients
it permits services to be provided without the training that would ordinarily be required
it permits services to continue after the emergency where the client prefers to remain in treatment
it requires that services end once the emergency has ended or appropriate services become available

questions.explanation: 2.02 requires discontinuation as soon as the emergency has ended or appropriate services are available. Client preference does not extend the authorization.

whyWrong.a: This is accurate — unavailability of alternatives is a condition of the provision.
whyWrong.b: This is accurate — the provision permits service without the appropriate training in an emergency.
whyWrong.d: This is accurate — it states the discontinuation requirement precisely.

questions.stem: A licensed psychologist retiring from clinical work joins a technology company to design a mental-health application, an area with no established training standards for psychologists. His obligations are governed chiefly by:

choices.text: Standard 2.02, since users of the software cannot access alternative providers directly
Standard 2.05, since the company's engineering team performs work that he has delegated
Standard 2.01(d), since no other qualified psychologist is available at the company
Standard 2.01(e), requiring reasonable steps to protect the welfare of those involved

questions.explanation: 2.01(e) governs work in emerging areas for which generally recognized preparatory training standards do not yet exist, requiring reasonable steps to protect the welfare of clients, students, and others involved.

whyWrong.a: 2.02 addresses emergencies, which product design is not.
whyWrong.b: Engineers are not performing psychological work delegated by him in the sense 2.05 contemplates.
whyWrong.c: 2.01(d) concerns requested services where no other provider is available to the recipient, not staffing at an employer.

questions.stem: Dr. Nasser, who has practised industrial-organizational psychology for fifteen years, wants to add clinical practice. He has completed a weekend workshop series on psychotherapy and proposes to begin seeing clients under monthly consultation. This plan is:

choices.text: inadequate, because a specialty change requires the subject-matter and skill requirements of doctoral training in it
adequate, because ongoing consultation supplies the supervised experience a specialty change demands
adequate, because 2.01 permits expansion of practice so long as potential harm to clients is minimized
inadequate, because a psychologist may never add a new specialty after completing the doctorate

questions.explanation: Adding a specialty requires meeting the same subject-matter and professional-skill requirements that apply to doctoral education, training, and experience in the new specialty. A workshop series and monthly consultation fall far short.

whyWrong.b: Consultation supplements training; it does not substitute for doctoral-level preparation in a new specialty.
whyWrong.c: 2.01 does permit expansion, but a change of specialty carries the heavier requirement described in the General Guidelines.
whyWrong.d: A specialty may be added; the requirement is substantive preparation, not a prohibition.

questions.stem: A psychologist supervising three practicum students learns that one has begun conducting a specialized assessment she has not trained him to administer, at the request of a school principal who says no one else can do it. The supervisor's obligation is best analysed under:

choices.text: 2.01(d), because the principal has represented that no other provider is available
2.05, because she must ensure delegated work is performed competently by the student
2.02, because the principal's urgency establishes the conditions of an emergency
2.06, because the student's willingness to exceed his training reflects a personal problem

questions.explanation: 2.05 places the duty on the psychologist who delegates work to ensure that the person performing it can do so competently, and the Code leaves that judgment to her. The student's competence to administer this assessment is hers to determine.

whyWrong.a: 2.01(d) concerns the psychologist's own provision of services, not her supervision of a trainee.
whyWrong.c: Administrative urgency is not the emergency 2.02 contemplates.
whyWrong.d: 2.06 concerns personal problems interfering with professional activity, which is not what is described.
